aarch64: fold with PMULL from 64 bytes (#78)

On CPUs with PMULL (the aes feature), fold the input with carry-less
multiplies, as the x86 code does with PCLMULQDQ, and finish with two
crc32x instructions instead of a Barrett reduction. Each fold of a stream
waits for the last, so the number of independent 128-bit streams grows
with the input: 4 from 64 bytes, 8 from 256 and 16 from 4 KiB.

When fewer than a round of input is left, the streams are halved, each of
the first half folded into its partner, down to one, taking what remains
of the input at each level: about log2(N) levels of latency rather than N
dependent folds. The last 0 to 15 bytes take at most one each of crc32x,
crc32w, crc32h and crc32b.

The fold constants come from x8n at compile time (combine::fold_keys); a
test checks them against the x86 constants.

Short inputs, and the PMULL check, stay in State::update: State stays
zero-sized, which makes hash() of 8 to 48 bytes 18-35% faster than
storing the feature in State or marking update #[inline]. EOR3 (SHA3) in
place of the two XORs made the 16-stream loop slower (79 against 95 GB/s
at 64 KiB), so it isn't used.

Apple M4, GB/s, three runs (1.5.4 -> this commit):

      8 B   4.0 ->  5.4      1023 B  11.8 ->  66.5
     32 B  11.7 -> 14.3      4095 B  21.7 ->  68.4
     64 B  28.1 -> 28-32     4096 B  22.3 ->  96.9
     96 B  25.8 -> 38.6     64 KiB   29.1 ->  99.8
    255 B  14.4 -> 60.3      1 MiB   31.7 -> 101.0

CPUs without PMULL take the crc32 chains as before. Tests cover both and
State's dispatch at lengths around every crossover and stride, and fail
on a wrong fold constant; fuzzing 16 million inputs up to 70 KB under
AddressSanitizer found nothing. The crate builds on 1.63, where this
module is compiled out, and on 1.89.

CI: check aarch64 kernel detection on known runners (#79)

A new test, `picks_the_expected_kernel`, compares what detection picks
("none", "crc" or "pmull") with `CRC32FAST_EXPECT`, and does nothing
when it is unset. The stable job sets it to "pmull" on the macOS
(Apple Silicon) runner and on a new native Linux arm64 runner, so a
change that silently stops using PMULL fails CI instead of passing with
less coverage. Linux arm64 was only tested under QEMU before.

CI: check the aarch64 target at the MSRV and on 1.80 (#80)

The msrv job only built for the runner's x86_64 target, so nothing
checked that the aarch64 code compiles on old toolchains. At the MSRV
aarch64 gets the baseline implementation, and 1.80 is the oldest rustc
that compiles the aarch64 kernels (where build.rs sets
`stable_arm_crc32_intrinsics`), so check both, with and without default
features. Checking needs only the target's standard library.
